key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the evidence of the father of the deceased (PW-4) regarding the alleged 'dying declaration' and the demand of gold karra by the appellant, but found that the investigation lacked credibility and did not focus on the contents of the complaint.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the credibility of PW-4 (father of the deceased) and PW-5 (Darshan Singh) as providing the main evidence, but noted that their testimony did not establish a proximate live link between the dowry demand and the death of the deceased.
bail_history: The appellant is on bail. The bail bond shall stand discharged.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 25.08.1997; Trial judgment: 11.08.2010; High Court decision: 11.08.2010; Supreme Court decision: 19.11.2014
legal_representation: Dinesh Kumar Garg, Ritu Puri, Advs. for the Appellant; Sanchar Anand, Kuldip Singh, Advs. for the Respondent
investigation_status: FIR registered under Section 304B IPC; charge sheet filed; investigation lacked credibility
procedural_irregularity: Investigation lacked credibility as it was not focused on the contents of the complaint and did not investigate the presence of aluminium phosphide poison
appeal_history: Trial court: Convicted under Section 304B IPC; High Court: Confirmed conviction; Supreme Court: Partly allowed the appeal, set aside conviction under Section 304B IPC, convicted under Section 498A IPC
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant-Baljinder Kaur demanded a gold karra as dowry two months after the marriage, which led to harassment and cruelty, thereby constituting a dowry death under Section 304B IPC. They also contended that the evidence of the dying declaration and the circumstances of the death supported the conviction.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the demand for a gold karra two months after the marriage was an isolated incident and not 'soon before her death', thus failing to establish the necessary proximity and live link required for a conviction under Section 304B IPC. They also emphasized that the investigation was flawed and the evidence was insufficient.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the proximity test, emphasizing that for a conviction under Section 304B IPC, there must be a proximate and live link between the cruelty or harassment related to dowry demand and the death of the victim, with the cruelty occurring 'soon before death'.
precedent_relied_upon: Hira Lal v. State (Govt. of NCT) Delhi 2003 (1) Suppl. SCR 734 : 2003 (8) SCC 80; Kamesh Panjiyar alias Kamlesh Panjiyar v. State of Bihar 2005 (1) SCR 903: (2005) 2 SCC 388; Thakkan Jha & Ors. v. State of Bihar (2004) 13 SCC 348; Baldev Singh v. State of Punjab 2008 (11) SCR 828 : (2008) 13 SCC 233
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed under Section 498A IPC, as the evidence on record made out an offence under that section. The appellant had already undergone a period of imprisonment, and the court considered the facts and circumstances of the case.
other_sentence_order: The appellant was convicted under Section 498A IPC and sentenced to undergo the period already undergone by her. The bail bond was discharged.
